title: The Witches of the Orient
text:
In the late 1950s the textile company Nichibo had a women's volleyball team at its Kaizuka factory near Osaka. Its players were company employees who worked shifts in the mill. Their coach, Daimatsu Hirobumi, a former army officer, set out to make them the best team in the world.

His training was famously severe. After a full day of factory work, the players trained late into the night, often until after midnight, every day of the year. Daimatsu drilled them in a diving, rolling technique for receiving hard spikes and getting back on their feet instantly, which made them almost impossible to score against. The players lived and trained together for years, sacrificing much of their personal lives.

In 1962, at the world championship in Moscow, the Nichibo players, forming most of Japan's national team, beat the Soviet Union in the deciding match to win the title. On a European tour the year before, foreign press had given them a nickname that stuck: the Witches of the Orient.

Women's volleyball made its Olympic debut at the 1964 Tokyo Games. On 23 October, in the final, Japan again faced the Soviet Union and won in three straight sets. A huge share of Japan's population watched on television, and the match became one of the most celebrated moments in the country's postwar recovery. Many of the players retired soon afterward to marry and start families.
lesson: Shared discipline and years of training together can forge a team that outplays taller, stronger rivals. Unity is built in the long hours no one sees.
people: Daimatsu Hirobumi, Kasai Masae, Nichibo Kaizuka players
source: Official Report of the Games of the XVIII Olympiad, Tokyo 1964; contemporary press reports
caveat: Daimatsu's harsh methods were controversial even at the time and would be widely criticized today.
